title: TB9-13883
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): He appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rendered on May 8, 2019, rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX is a citizen of India. He appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rendered on May 8, 2019, rejecting his claim for refugee protection.

The Appellant claims that he is gay and fears persecution or harm from his family and community in India. He argues that the RPD erred in rejecting his claim based on overriding concerns regarding the credibility of his evidence.

I dismiss the appeal. After considering the Appellant's submissions and all the evidence, I find that the Appellant failed to establish his credibility on a balance of probabilities which is determinative of the appeal.1 BACKGROUND
According to his Basis of Claim form (BOC), the Appellant was disowned, disinherited and rejected by his family and Sikh community in India because he is gay.

The Appellant states that in XXXX XXXX, his same-sex relationship was revealed to his parents in India. As a result, the Appellant was mistreated and threatened by his father, male family members and his community. He ended his same-sex relationship in XXXX XXXX.
The Appellant's parents arranged for the Appellant to come to Canada XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX to separate him from his boyfriend and spare him ill-treatment as a result of his sexual orientation in India.
The Appellant came to Canada XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Following his arrival, the Appellant had various same-sex relationships including his partner XXXX XXXX."
The Appellant made a refugee claim on April 5, 2018. Then, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, he got married to a XXXX XXXX with whom he has a relationship.
The RPD rejected the Appellant's refugee claim based on overriding concerns with the credibility of his evidence.
The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in its credibility assessment. ADMISSIBILITY OF NEW EVIDENCE PRESENTED ON APPEAL

The Appellant requests to submit new evidence to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). According to ss. 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Appellant may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of his claim, or that was not reasonably available, or that the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection. The RAD does not have discretion to admit new evidence if it does not meet one of the conditions set out in ss. 110(4).2
Item 1 is a sworn Affidavit from the Appellant dated June 15, 2019. Item 1 also includes attached documents which already form part of the RPD record.

Item 1 appears to deconstruct and criticize the RPD's decision. The IRPA expressly limits admissible evidence to new evidence or evidence that was not reasonably available or obtainable at the time the claim was rejected. The affidavit is not new evidence. Rather, I will treat it as supplementary submissions in the present appeal.

The Memorandum of Appeal also indicates that a sworn affidavit from the Appellant's wife will be submitted as new evidence to support his sexual orientation and "help change the negative decision" by the RPD.3 However, I note that a letter or affidavit from the Appellant's wife does not form part of the record before the RAD.
While the Appellant requests an oral hearing before the RAD, there is no new evidence admissible on appeal. This, in itself, is a bar to an oral hearing in the present case.4 SCOPE OF THE RAD APPEAL
paragraphs.heading_before: REQUEST FOR A HEARING BEFORE THE RAD

paragraphs.text: The RAD reviews decisions on a standard of correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it.5 Deference may be required when the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in the assessment of the credibility of oral evidence.6 I have applied the correctness standard in the present case. ANALYSIS The RPD did not demonstrate bias

The Appellant submits that the RPD demonstrated bias in reaching the decision to reject his claim. It is argued that the RPD decided at the outset of the hearing that the Appellant is not worthy of Canada's protection. Then, the Panel member proceeded to engage in an exercise where he dismissed oral and documentary evidence in an arbitrary way to support his conclusion that the Appellant is not credible.
I find this submission is unfounded.

First, it bears noting that an allegation of bias against a tribunal is a serious allegation which must meet a very high threshold and requires cogent evidence.7 As explained by the Federal Court of Appeal in Arthur, It challenges the integrity of the tribunal and of its members who participated in the impugned decision. It cannot be done lightly. It cannot rest on mere suspicion, pure conjecture, insinuations or mere impressions of an applicant or his counsel. It must be supported by material evidence demonstrating conduct that derogates from the standard.8
In the present case, the Appellant asserts that the RPD was biased. This being said, the Appellant has not directed me to any material evidence demonstrating bias.

My own review of the audio recording of the RPD hearing does not raise any concerns with the manner of questioning adopted by the Panel member during the RPD hearing. To the contrary, he posed questions in both a respectful and direct manner, compatible with the SOGIE guidelines and his role as a decision maker in an inquisitorial process. Likewise, there is nothing perceptible in the record to suggest that the RPD derogated from acceptable standards of conduct in reaching the decision to reject the claim.
In sum, my review of the record reveals no evidence of bias in the present case. The RPD did not err in finding that the Appellant's evidence lacked credibility
The RPD dismissed the claim, finding overriding concerns with the credibility of the Appellant's evidence that he is gay and fears persecution or harm from his family and community in India.

The RPD reached this finding based on the following: - The Appellant states in his BOC that he fled India because of ill-treatment stemming from his sexual orientation as a gay or homosexual man. He emphasized that a person cannot change who he is and he fears continued mistreatment from his family and community in India. When asked to explain what being gay meant to him, the Appellant stated that this is a natural phenomenon and that he only likes boys. - In contrast, the Appellant provided a marriage certificate revealing that he married XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. When asked to explain why he married a woman if he is gay, he stated that he and his wife are bisexual, and they are in the process of getting to know each other. When challenged to explain why he refers to himself as bisexual when he previously explained that he is homosexual, the Appellant stated that homosexuality and bisexuality is the same thing. Further in his testimony, he reverted to calling himself gay. - The RPD reached a negative inference from the Appellant's evolving testimony. Moreover, the RPD found that the Appellant's marriage to a woman undermines the credibility of his claim that he is gay. The RPD rejected the Appellant's assertion that he is bisexual. While the Appellant testified that there is no distinction between gays and bisexuals, other aspects of his testimony revealed that he clearly differentiated between these two types of relationships. For instance, during his testimony he referred to his wife as bisexual and himself as gay. - The RPD also reached an adverse inference about the Appellant's sexual orientation because the Appellant did not provide any letters of support from his XXXX XXXX to corroborate the central allegation that her husband is gay or bisexual. - The Appellant testified that prior to his marriage, he had a same-sex relationship with XXXX XXXX XXXX in Canada. The Appellant stated they met in May 2018. The RPD noted that this is incorrect given that the BOC (which refers to his relationship with XXXX XXXX XXXX) is signed April 2018. In response, the Appellant stated that he could not remember the date he met this man and could not remember the last time they spoke. The RPD found the Appellant's credibility about his sexual orientation is further impugned given his lack of knowledge about someone he alleges to have had an intimate relationship with and the lack of corroboration to establish their relationship. - The Appellant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and signed his refugee claim around XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The RPD found that the delay in making his refugee claim undermined the credibility of his subjective fear. Considering that the Appellant XXXX XXXX XXXX; considering his allegation that he fears being killed in India and considering that he only attended XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX which placed him in a precarious situation at risk of removal, the RPD found the credibility of his subjective fear is undermined by his delay in making his refugee claim. - Finally, the RPD noted a significant omission which is not reasonably explained. On the one hand, the Appellant declared in his BOC that he was beaten by his parents and threatened with death by male family members after they learned of his sexual orientation in India. When he testified, he added that he went to the Indian police to report that he was mistreated by his family but ended up being revictimized by the police. When challenged to explain this omission from his BOC, he stated that he did not mention the incident involving the police because he had already provided many details. The RPD found that a significant omission which is not reasonably explained further impugns the Appellant's credibility.

On appeal, Counsel submits that the RPD ignored testimony and evidence properly placed before him and "engaged in a perverse and patently unreasonable line of reasoning and decision making".9 It is also argued that the RPD engaged in an improper analysis of the testimony and evidence by ignoring truthful evidence and engaging in speculation to bolster the negative credibility finding.10

While I agree that it is improper for any decision maker to reach a decision by ignoring evidence and engaging in speculation, the Appellant has not provided any substantive evidence to demonstrate how the RPD erred in its analysis in the present case. Rather, the submissions advanced by Counsel are merely bald assertions unsupported by the evidence.

To be clear, the Appellant asserts in the Memorandum of Appeal that the most notable errors made by the RPD are found at paragraphs 6,8,9, 10-16 and 18-22 of the RPD's decision. Considering that the entire decision is 24 paragraphs long and that the credibility analysis begins at paragraph 6 of the decision, it appears that the Appellant is submitting that the entirety of the credibility analysis conducted by the RPD is flawed and unsustainable. However, the Appellant has failed to provide any specific information about the nature of any errors made by the RPD.

My own review of the record reveals that the analysis conducted by the RPD was properly informed by the SOGIE Guidelines11 which sets out guiding principles for decision makers adjudicating cases involving SOGIE at the Immigration Refugee Board. As noted above, I find that the RPD approached the claim with sensitivity and gave the Appellant every opportunity to establish facts underpinning his claim, including any challenges he faced in India as a result of his non-conformity to SOGIE norms.

I am mindful of the fact that sexual orientation claims may present evidentiary challenges for the claimant and decision maker, given the inherently private nature of the claims.12 However, this does not mean that the RPD should simply disregard credibility concerns that arise from the evidence. It is worth noting that the SOGIE Guidelines explain that decision makers may draw a negative inference from vague testimony as well as material inconsistencies and omissions in the evidence that have no reasonable explanation.13

The crux of the present refugee claim centers on the Appellant's assertion that he is gay and was victimized, rejected and threatened by his family and community after his same-sex relationship was exposed. For this reason, he alleges that he fears returning to India.

My review of the record is compatible with the RPD's. The Appellant provided evolving testimony about his sexual orientation and there were significant inconsistencies and omissions in the evidence striking at the heart of his claim that he is gay and fears harm in India. I also agree with the RPD who found that the Appellant's subjective fear lacked credibility based on his 14-month delay in making his refugee claim which placed him in a precarious situation in Canada once he abandoned his schooling.

The marriage certificate is compelling evidence that the Appellant is in a relationship with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. While the Appellant asserts that his relationship with this woman is "developing" and that they are both bisexual, he made no attempt to corroborate the nature of his relationship with his wife who remained at home on the day of the RPD hearing. The RPD did not err in reaching a negative inference as a result of the Appellant's failure to provide a letter of support or produce his wife as a witness to clarify or corroborate the nature of their relationship. I also note that no information from the Appellant's wife is forthcoming on appeal.
Overall, I conclude that the RPD did not err in finding overriding concerns with the Appellant's credibility which is determinative of the appeal.

For all these reasons, I confirm the decision of the RPD in accordance with ss. 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, namely that the Appellant is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection". The appeal is dismissed.
